clue1.note: Opens with a bare 'Here' instead of saying what kind of thing the answer is.
clue1.fix: On this planet a day lasts longer than a year, and the Sun rises in the west.

judge.summary: Strong, well-ordered facts; only clue 1 needs to open with 'On this planet' instead of a bare 'Here'.

clue1.note: 'She ruled Egypt' gives the answer at once, and 'never spoke her subjects' language until she chose to' is muddled.
clue1.fix: This ruler, of Macedonian Greek descent, could speak with most foreign envoys without an interpreter, Plutarch wrote, and was the first of the family to learn Egyptian.

clue3.note: Julius Caesar and Mark Antony give the answer away at once.
clue3.fix: Following royal custom, she married two of her younger brothers in turn, and each shared her throne.

judge.summary: Clues 1 and 3 give the answer at once ('She ruled Egypt', Caesar and Antony), and clue 1's language fact is muddled.

clue1.note: A verbless fragment that never says what kind of thing the answer is, and its arm-neuron fact repeats clue 3.
clue1.fix: This animal has three hearts and blue blood that gets its color from copper rather than iron.

clue3.note: Repeats clue 1's point that most of its neurons are in the arms.
clue3.fix: Some species can shed an arm to escape a predator and grow it back, and a mother often stops eating while she guards her eggs, dying soon after they hatch.

judge.summary: Clue 1 is a fragment with no 'This animal', and its arm-neuron fact is repeated in clue 3.

clue1.note: Refers to the answer only as 'here' instead of opening with 'This city'.
clue1.fix: This city was the nation's capital when George Washington was sworn in here as the first U.S. president in 1789.

clue2.note: Naming Albany gives the answer away at once.
clue2.fix: It is the most populous city in its country, yet it is not even the capital of its own state.

clue3.note: Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx and Ellis Island are instant giveaways before clue 4.
clue3.fix: Dutch settlers supposedly bought the island at its heart from the Lenape people in 1626 for goods worth 60 guilders.

judge.summary: Albany in clue 2 and the five boroughs in clue 3 give the city away early, so it plays easy.
Four distinct facts in a sensible order, led by the striking polar hexagon.
Distinct, specific facts that get easier in a sensible order.
Four distinct, surprising facts in a sensible order from blue sunsets to the giveaway.
Four separate angles (death in France, anatomy, mirror writing, Mona Lisa) in a sound order.
Four distinct, accurate and interesting facts (the sitter, the 1963 US tour, the 1911 theft, the Louvre) that get easier in a sensible order.
Early careers, the letters to Theo and his output are distinct facts in a sensible order, with the famous works saved for clue 4.

clue1.note: Opens with a bare 'His'; say 'This physicist's'.
clue1.fix: This physicist's most famous theory never won him a Nobel Prize; the award instead cited his work on the photoelectric effect.

clue3.note: Relativity is his best-known work and gives the answer at once.
clue3.fix: In 1905, while working as a patent clerk in Bern, he published four papers that reshaped physics.

judge.summary: Good first two clues; clue 3 (relativity) is instant and clue 1 needs 'This physicist's'.

clue1.note: Opens with a bare 'He'; say 'This scientist'.
clue1.fix: This scientist spent as many years on alchemy and biblical prophecy as on physics, and while running England's Royal Mint he sent counterfeiters to the gallows.

clue3.note: The laws of motion and the falling apple give the answer at once.
clue3.fix: He split white light into a rainbow with prisms and built the first practical reflecting telescope.

judge.summary: Strong opening clues; clue 3 (laws of motion and the apple) is instant and clue 1 needs 'This scientist'.

clue1.note: Opens with a bare 'She'; say 'This scientist'.
clue1.fix: This scientist remains the only person ever to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences.

clue3.note: Discovering polonium and radium gives the answer at once.
clue3.fix: She named the first element she discovered after her homeland, which was not an independent country at the time.

judge.summary: Clue 3 (polonium and radium) is instant, and clue 1 needs to say 'This scientist' instead of 'She'.

clue1.note: Opens with a bare 'Its'; say 'This peak's'.
clue1.fix: This peak's summit is not the point on Earth's surface farthest from the planet's center; a peak in Ecuador wins that because Earth bulges at the equator.

clue3.note: Hillary and Tenzing's 1953 climb gives the answer at once.
clue3.fix: Its summit is made of limestone holding fossils of sea creatures from an ancient ocean floor.

judge.summary: Clue 3 (Hillary and Tenzing) is instant, and clue 1 needs to name the kind of thing.

clue1.note: Opens with a bare 'it'; say 'this desert'.
clue1.fix: Dust lifted from this desert blows clear across the Atlantic to fertilize the Amazon rainforest thousands of miles away.

clue3.note: 'Sprawling across North Africa' gives the answer at once.
clue3.fix: Snow has dusted the dunes near the Algerian town of Aïn Séfra on its northern edge several times since 1979.

judge.summary: Clue 3 ('across North Africa') is instant, and clue 1 needs to say 'this desert'.

clue1.note: Doesn't say what kind of thing the answer is, and 'smothered in ice' makes it close to instant.
clue1.fix: This continent is technically the world's largest desert, because so little snow or rain falls on it each year.

clue3.note: The coldest temperature ever recorded points straight to the answer.
clue3.fix: It locks up about 70% of the world's fresh water, and its ice sheet is more than 4 kilometers thick in places.

judge.summary: Every early clue points straight at the answer; clue 1 needs 'This continent' and clue 3's coldest-temperature record is instant.

clue1.note: Doesn't say what kind of thing the answer is; say 'this waterfall'.
clue1.fix: In 1901 a 63-year-old schoolteacher rode over this waterfall sealed inside a wooden barrel, and lived.

clue2.note: Only the smaller American Falls was dried out in 1969, not the whole landmark.
clue2.fix: In 1969 engineers dammed off its smaller American section for several months, leaving that cliff face dry so they could study erosion.

clue3.note: A US-Canada border spot for honeymooners and daredevils gives the answer at once.
clue3.fix: Its river carries water from Lake Erie to Lake Ontario, and its brink has worn back about 11 kilometers over some 12,000 years.

judge.summary: Clue 3 is instant, clue 2 overstates the 1969 shutdown (only the American Falls ran dry), and clue 1 needs 'this waterfall'.

clue1.note: Opens with a bare 'It'; say what kind of thing the answer is.
clue1.fix: This natural wonder is the largest structure on Earth built by living creatures, and it can be seen from space.

clue3.note: The Queensland, Australia location gives the answer at once and repeats clue 4.
clue3.fix: It is made up of nearly 3,000 separate reefs, and Captain Cook's ship Endeavour ran aground on it in 1770.

judge.summary: Clue 3's Queensland location is instant and repeats clue 4; clue 1 needs to say what kind of thing it is.

clue2.note: The exposed rock layers are the canyon's best-known feature, so this is easier than the Roosevelt clue after it.
clue2.fix: On his first visit in 1903, Theodore Roosevelt urged 'Leave it as it is,' and in 1908 he made this landmark a national monument.

clue3.note: Less well known than the rock-layers clue before it, so the two should swap.
clue3.fix: This landmark's walls show a largely undisturbed cross section of Earth's crust reaching back some two billion years.

judge.summary: Strong, accurate facts, but clues 2 and 3 should swap because the two-billion-year rock layers are better known than Roosevelt's 1903 visit.

clue1.note: Opens with a bare 'It', and the usual figure is up to 15 cm, not more than 15 cm.
clue1.fix: This landmark can grow up to 15 centimeters taller in summer, when the heat makes its iron expand.

clue2.note: Shares the 1889 world's fair with clue 4; fix clue 4 rather than this one.

clue3.note: An iron lattice towering over a European capital gives the answer at once.
clue3.fix: Its designer built himself a small private apartment near the top, where he once hosted Thomas Edison.

clue4.note: Repeats clue 2's 1889 world's fair.
clue4.fix: This wrought-iron landmark on the Champ de Mars is one of the most visited monuments on Earth and a symbol of Paris.

judge.summary: Clue 3 is instant, clue 4 repeats clue 2's 1889 world's fair, and clue 1 needs 'This landmark' and 'up to' 15 cm.
Four distinct facts, sensibly ordered, each needing a moment's thought.

clue1.note: Doesn't say what kind of thing the answer is, and 'a gift between two nations' repeats clue 4.
clue1.fix: This monument's copper skin was a shiny reddish brown when new, before the weather turned it green.

clue3.note: A torch-bearing figure in New York Harbor gives the answer at once.
clue3.fix: Its sculptor, Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi, is said to have modeled its face on his mother's.

judge.summary: Clue 3 (torch in New York Harbor) is instant, and clue 1's 'gift between two nations' repeats clue 4.
Three vivid, lesser-known facts lead well into a clear giveaway.

clue1.note: Opens with a bare 'It', and 'physically cannot walk backward' overstates a popular claim.
clue1.fix: This animal can't easily move backward, and springy tendons let it hop faster without burning more energy.

clue3.note: A marsupial that leans on its tail and kicks gives the answer at once.
clue3.fix: A group of them is called a mob, and when moving slowly they use their thick tail as a fifth leg.

clue4.note: Dangling opening: 'Australia's famous hopping icon' attaches to 'the males', not to the animal.
clue4.fix: This hopping Australian icon has males called boomers and babies called joeys.

judge.summary: Clue 3 (tail and kick) is instant and clue 4 has a dangling opening phrase.

clue1.note: Bamboo gives the answer away at once and repeats clue 4.
clue1.fix: For over a century scientists argued whether this animal was a raccoon relative, until DNA showed it is a true bear.

clue3.note: China's black-and-white bears give the answer at once and repeat clue 4.
clue3.fix: A sixth 'finger' formed from an enlarged wrist bone helps it grip the stalks it eats.

judge.summary: Bamboo in clue 1 and China's black-and-white bears in clue 3 give the answer at once and repeat clue 4.

clue1.note: Opens with a bare 'Its'; say 'This reptile's'.
clue1.fix: This reptile's two eyes can swivel and aim in different directions at the same instant.

clue3.note: Color change is its defining trait, so this gives the answer at once and repeats clue 4.
clue3.fix: Its curling tail grips branches like an extra hand, and the smallest species could sit on a fingertip.

judge.summary: Clue 3's color change is the defining trait, gives the answer away and repeats clue 4.

clue1.note: Opens with a bare 'It'; say 'This insect'.
clue1.fix: This insect tells its sisters where to find food by performing a looping 'waggle dance.'

clue3.note: A queen-led colony building six-sided wax cells gives the answer at once.
clue3.fix: Workers keep the hive's core near 35°C, and in winter they huddle and shiver their flight muscles to stay warm.

judge.summary: Clue 3 (queen, wax combs) is instant, and clue 1 needs 'This insect'.
Hearing, teeth and self-awareness are three surprising, distinct facts.

clue1.note: Opens with a bare 'its'; say 'this drink's'.
clue1.fix: Legend credits this drink's discovery to an Ethiopian goatherd who saw his flock dancing after nibbling certain red berries.

clue3.note: Espresso, cappuccino and latte give the answer at once.
clue3.fix: Mecca banned it in 1511, and an Ottoman sultan later shut the houses that served it, fearing they bred dissent.

judge.summary: Clue 3 (espresso, cappuccino, latte) gives the answer away; clue 1 needs 'this drink's'.

clue2.note: 'Pressed' is imprecise, since chocolate is ground from the beans, and the clue is mostly a description of what it is made from.
clue2.fix: Made from the fermented, roasted seeds of a tropical tree, this treat melts just below human body temperature.

clue3.note: Most players know chocolate is poisonous to dogs, so the clue is instant.
clue3.fix: The tree whose seeds make this treat is named Theobroma, Greek for 'food of the gods'.

judge.summary: The dogs detail in clue 3 gives the answer away, and clue 2 reads as a description.
Four distinct, true facts in a sensible order, with the Decca rejection as a strong opener.

clue3.note: Naming 'Für Elise' gives the answer away at once, since most players know who wrote it.
clue3.fix: This composer wrote only one opera, 'Fidelio', and reworked it several times over about a decade before its final version succeeded in 1814.

judge.summary: Clue 3 names 'Für Elise', which settles the question before clue 4.
Solid, accurate facts from four angles, though the answer is easy to reach by clue 2.

clue1.note: Opens with a bare 'its', and the Shibuya scramble repeats clue 4.
clue1.fix: This city's Shinjuku Station is the busiest in the world, handling more than 3 million passengers a day.

clue3.note: Hosting the 1964 and 2021 Summer Olympics gives the answer at once.
clue3.fix: The most populous metropolitan area on the planet, it is home to roughly 37 million people.

judge.summary: Clue 1's Shibuya scramble repeats clue 4, and clue 3's two Olympics give the answer at once.

clue1.note: Opens with a bare 'Its'; say 'This animal's'.
clue1.fix: This animal's nursing calf packs on roughly the weight of an adult human every single day.

clue2.note: Sperm whale clicks are louder, so 'the loudest sounds made by any animal' is doubtful.
clue2.fix: Its heart alone is about the size of a small car, and its low calls can travel hundreds of kilometers underwater.

judge.summary: A good question; clue 1 needs 'This animal's' and clue 2's 'loudest animal' claim is doubtful because sperm whales are louder.

clue1.note: Electric sense is shared by all sharks, great whites don't usually hunt prey buried in sand, and it opens with a bare 'its'.
clue1.fix: A tagged female of this fish, nicknamed Nicole, swam from South Africa to Australia and back in about nine months.

judge.summary: Clue 1's electric sense fits all sharks, and its sand-hunting detail is doubtful for great whites.

clue2.note: 'First Consul' plus the Louisiana sale gives the name at once, and it is easier than clue 3.
clue2.fix: In 1805 this commander was crowned King of Italy in Milan with the old Iron Crown of Lombardy.

judge.summary: Clue 2 is instant and easier than clue 3, so replace it with a less familiar fact such as the 1805 Italian coronation.

clue1.note: Opens with a bare 'it'; say 'this peak'.
clue1.fix: Hokusai gave this peak a whole series of woodblock prints, among them one of a towering, claw-like wave.

clue3.note: The highest peak in its country, visible from Tokyo, gives the answer at once.
clue3.fix: On its northwest flank lies Aokigahara, a forest so dense and quiet it is nicknamed the Sea of Trees.

judge.summary: Clue 3 (highest peak, visible from Tokyo) is instant; clue 1 needs 'this peak'.

clue3.note: 'Peruvian Andes' names the place outright, so most players answer at once.
clue3.fix: American explorer Hiram Bingham brought this site to the world's attention in 1911, after a local farmer led him up to it.

judge.summary: A great beer-commercial opener, but clue 3's 'Peruvian Andes' makes it instant before clue 4.

clue1.note: Opens with a bare 'it', and many great rivers flow north, so 'unlike most great rivers' is a myth.
clue1.fix: This river flows north for thousands of kilometers before fanning out into a huge delta on the Mediterranean.

clue2.note: Feeding an early civilization repeats clue 4's 'lifeblood of ancient Egypt'.
clue2.fix: The Aswan High Dam, finished in 1970, ended its yearly floods and created one of the world's largest artificial lakes.

judge.summary: Clue 1's 'unlike most great rivers' is a myth, and clue 2 repeats clue 4's ancient-Egypt angle.

clue1.note: Opens with a bare 'He'; say 'This naturalist'.
clue1.fix: This naturalist sat on his world-changing theory for some twenty years before he dared to publish it.

clue2.note: HMS Beagle and the Galápagos finches give the answer at once.
clue2.fix: Before marrying his cousin Emma Wedgwood, he wrote out a list of the pros and cons of marriage.

clue3.note: Natural selection is his best-known idea, gives the answer at once, and overlaps clue 4's theory of evolution.
clue3.fix: He spent eight years studying barnacles, and his face appeared on the Bank of England's ten-pound note.

judge.summary: Clues 2 and 3 (the Beagle, natural selection) give the answer at once.
A surprising fashion opener, then an organization, a quote and her disappearance, each a different angle in the right order.

clue1.note: The Margherita gives the answer away at once, and it opens with a bare 'Its'.
clue1.fix: In 2017 UNESCO added the craft of this dish's Naples-style makers to its list of the world's intangible cultural heritage.

clue3.note: A 'Hawaiian' style topped with pineapple gives the answer at once.
clue3.fix: One of its most argued-over styles was invented not in the tropics but in Canada, by a Greek-born cook in 1962.

judge.summary: Clues 1 and 3 (Margherita, Hawaiian) each give the answer at once.

clue1.note: The peach-basket origin is widely known and easier than clue 2, so it should come second.
clue1.fix: At the 1936 Berlin Olympics this sport's first gold-medal game was played outdoors on a converted clay tennis court in driving rain.

clue2.note: Harder than clue 1; swap the two.
clue2.fix: This sport's first goals were two peach containers hung from a gym balcony rail with their bottoms still in, so the ball had to be retrieved after every score.

judge.summary: Swap clues 1 and 2 so the well-known peach-basket origin is not the opening clue.

clue1.note: Opens with a bare 'It'; say 'This animal'.
clue1.fix: This animal sleeps with only half its brain at a time, keeping one eye open so it remembers to surface for air.

judge.summary: Strong facts throughout; only clue 1 needs to open with 'This animal'.

clue1.note: Opens with a bare 'Its'; say 'This bird's'.
clue1.fix: This bird's eyes are fixed in their sockets, so it swivels its head as much as three-quarters of the way around to look about.

clue3.note: Coughing up pellets gives the answer at once, and the sound-funneling face repeats clue 2's hearing.
clue3.fix: A group of them is called a parliament, and young burrowing ones can mimic a rattlesnake's rattle to scare off predators.

judge.summary: Clue 3's pellets give the answer at once, and its face-as-ear-funnel repeats clue 2's hearing.

clue1.note: Opens with a bare 'It', and 'moves so little' all but names the answer.
clue1.fix: Green algae grows in this mammal's fur, tinting it a mossy color that helps it hide in the treetops.

judge.summary: Good facts, but clue 1's 'moves so little' all but names the answer and it needs 'this mammal'.

clue1.note: Opens with a bare 'Its', and 'among these cats' is awkward.
clue1.fix: This cat's roar can carry as far as five miles, and in its family groups the females do most of the hunting.

clue2.note: Living in prides gives the answer at once.
clue2.fix: It can sleep up to 20 hours a day, and a new male taking over a group often kills the cubs sired by his rival.

clue3.note: The male's mane gives the answer at once.
clue3.fix: Wild ones survive in Asia only in India's Gir Forest, though the species once ranged into Europe.

judge.summary: Clues 2 and 3 (prides, the mane) give the answer at once, and clue 1's wording is awkward.

clue1.note: Opens with a bare 'it'; say 'this metal'.
clue1.fix: Nearly all of this metal ever mined would fit inside just a few Olympic swimming pools, and much of it was forged in colliding neutron stars.

clue3.note: The symbol Au and carats give the answer at once.
clue3.fix: Thin flakes of it are sprinkled on luxury desserts as an edible garnish, and it passes through the body untouched.

judge.summary: Clue 3 (Au and carats) gives the answer at once; clue 1 needs 'this metal'.

clue1.note: Opens with a bare 'it'; say what kind of thing the answer is.
clue1.fix: For a split second this flash heats the air around it to roughly five times the temperature of the Sun's surface.

clue2.note: Explaining thunder gives the answer at once and builds on clue 1's superheated air.
clue2.fix: Erupting volcanoes can produce it too, as grinding ash particles build up electric charge.

clue3.note: A skyscraper being 'struck' gives the answer at once.
clue3.fix: When it hits sand, it can fuse the grains into hollow glass tubes called fulgurites.

judge.summary: Clue 2 (thunder) and clue 3 (a building being struck) give the answer at once.
A strong, surprising opener followed by distinct facts in a good order.

clue1.note: Opens with a bare 'It', and 'no ordinary streets for cars' makes it close to instant.
clue1.fix: This city rests on millions of wooden posts driven deep into the mud of a lagoon.

clue2.note: A sinking Italian city where people get around by boat gives the answer at once.
clue2.fix: Its glassmakers were ordered onto the nearby island of Murano in 1291, partly to keep their furnaces' fires away from the city.

clue3.note: The Grand Canal, gondolas and St. Mark's Square give the answer at once.
clue3.fix: In 2024 it became the first city in the world to charge day-trippers an entry fee on its busiest days.

judge.summary: Clues 2 and 3 (boats, gondolas, St. Mark's) give the answer at once, and clue 1's 'no streets for cars' comes close to it.

clue1.note: Opens with a bare 'its'; say 'this city's'.
clue1.fix: Beneath this city's streets wind tunnels stacked with the bones of some six million people.

clue2.note: The 'one stop sign' claim is popular but shaky, and the boulevards half is vague.
clue2.fix: Its grand boulevards were cut through crowded medieval streets in the 1850s and 1860s under Baron Haussmann.

clue3.note: The Louvre and Notre-Dame give the answer at once.
clue3.fix: Its first metro line opened in 1900, and many of its subway entrances still carry Art Nouveau signs by Hector Guimard.

judge.summary: Clue 3 (Louvre, Notre-Dame) is instant and clue 2's one-stop-sign claim is shaky.

clue1.note: Opens with a bare 'its'; say 'this monument's'.
clue1.fix: Some of this monument's stones were hauled roughly 150 miles from the hills of Wales, though no one is certain how.

clue3.note: Salisbury Plain and a ring of standing stones give the answer at once.
clue3.fix: Standing on Salisbury Plain in England, it was bought at auction in 1915 by a local man for £6,600.

judge.summary: Clue 3 (Salisbury Plain, ring of stones) is instant; clue 1 needs 'this monument's'.
Four distinct, well-ordered facts with a strong opener about the Lincoln Cathedral spire.

clue1.note: Opens with a bare 'Its' instead of saying what kind of thing the answer is.
clue1.fix: This building's architect quit in a bitter row with the government and never came back to see it finished.

clue3.note: White sail-like shells beside an Australian harbor give it away, and clue 4 repeats the sails.
clue3.fix: Its roof is covered in more than a million glossy tiles made in Sweden, and Queen Elizabeth II opened it in 1973.

clue4.note: Uses 'Sydney' from the answer's name.
clue4.fix: This sail-roofed performing-arts centre beside the Harbour Bridge is Australia's most recognizable building.

judge.summary: The first two clues are strong, but clue 3's sail roof is instant and repeated in clue 4, which also says 'Sydney'.

clue4.note: 'Last queen of France before the revolution' is a little loose, since she was still queen during it.
clue4.fix: This French queen, wrongly credited with saying 'Let them eat cake,' was sent to the guillotine in 1793.

judge.summary: Four distinct, well-ordered facts, from her play farm at Versailles to her execution.

clue1.note: The story that he signed the Secret Service into law the day he was shot is poorly supported; the agency began in July 1865.
clue1.fix: This future president is the only one ever to hold a U.S. patent, for a device to lift boats over shallow water.

clue3.note: The Civil War and the Emancipation Proclamation make this instant.
clue3.fix: The first Republican elected president, he was born in a one-room log cabin in Kentucky.

judge.summary: Clue 1 rests on a shaky Secret Service story and should say who 'he' is, and clue 3 is instant.

clue1.note: The bicycle shop is better known than clue 2's wing fact, and it opens with a bare 'They'.
clue1.fix: These inventors' real breakthrough was not the engine but 'wing warping', twisting the wings to steer and keep balance.

clue2.note: Less known than clue 1, so the two should swap.
clue2.fix: They ran a bicycle shop in Dayton, Ohio, and paid for their flying experiments with its profits.

clue3.note: North Carolina and 1903 make the first-flight clue instant.
clue3.fix: Neither of them ever married, and they tossed a coin to decide which would try to fly first.

judge.summary: Clues 1 and 2 should swap, clue 1 should say who 'they' are, and clue 3 is instant.

clue1.note: Beating 'most supercars' is overstated, and the speed angle repeats clue 3 and points straight to the answer.
clue1.fix: This cat cannot roar; instead it chirps like a bird and purrs like a house cat.

clue3.note: 'Fastest land animal' is instant, and research has challenged the idea that it stops because it overheats.
clue3.fix: It uses its long tail like a rudder to make sharp turns while chasing gazelles at full speed.

judge.summary: Speed drives both clue 1 and clue 3, so the question gives itself away early.

clue1.note: An egg-laying mammal with a venom spur is its best-known fact, so clue 1 is instant; it also opens with a bare 'It'.
clue1.fix: This animal glows blue-green under ultraviolet light, which scientists only reported in 2020.

judge.summary: Clue 1 leads with the most famous fact and gives the answer away; the other three clues are strong.

clue1.note: 'Towering neck' gives it away, and it never says what kind of thing 'it' is.
clue1.fix: This animal has exactly seven bones in its neck, the same number as a mouse or a human.

clue3.note: 'The tallest animal on Earth' is instant.
clue3.fix: It may sleep as little as half an hour a day, and its heart can weigh about 11 kilograms.

judge.summary: Clue 1's towering neck and clue 3's 'tallest animal' both give the answer away too early.

clue1.note: Losing its planet status in 2006 is its most famous fact, so clue 1 is instant.
clue1.fix: This world was named in 1930 by an 11-year-old English schoolgirl, who suggested the name over breakfast.

clue4.note: Swap with clue 1 so the demotion becomes the giveaway.
clue4.fix: This icy world, discovered in 1930, counted as the ninth planet until it was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006.

judge.summary: Clue 1 leads with the demotion, the best-known fact; swap it with clue 4's naming story.

clue3.note: Ozone plus atomic number 8 names the element at once.
clue3.fix: Antoine Lavoisier named this element from Greek words meaning 'acid former', wrongly believing every acid contained it.

judge.summary: Clue 3 gives the answer away with ozone and atomic number 8; the other clues are strong.

clue1.note: Opens with a bare 'It', and it is easier than the vaguer clue 2.
clue1.fix: No two people ever see exactly the same one of these sights, because it depends on where the light meets each person's eyes.

clue2.note: Harder than clue 1, so the two should swap.
clue2.fix: It is really a full circle of light, but from the ground you only see the top arc.

clue3.note: Describes how it forms rather than giving a fact, and gives the answer away.
clue3.fix: Sometimes a fainter second one appears just outside it, with its colours in reverse order.

judge.summary: Clue 3 describes how it forms instead of giving a fact, and clue 1 is easier than clue 2.
Great facts, though the generic answer means most players will get it on clue 1.

clue1.note: Opens with a bare 'It' instead of saying what kind of thing the answer is.
clue1.fix: This country sits across two tectonic plates that are drifting apart, so it grows about 2 cm wider each year.

clue2.note: Packs two unrelated facts, its hydropower comes from rivers rather than waterfalls, and mosquitoes were found there for the first time in 2025.
clue2.fix: About nine in ten of its homes are heated with hot water piped up from underground.

clue3.note: 'Land of fire and ice' contains 'ice' and 'land' from the answer's name.
clue3.fix: Its parliament, first held in the year 930, is often called the oldest in the world still meeting.

judge.summary: Clue 3 says 'land of fire and ice', which contains the answer's name, and clue 2 packs two facts, one now out of date.

clue3.note: The opening phrase dangles and does not name what kind of thing the answer is.
